passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传： 秦王立一年，薨，谥为孝文王。太子子楚代立，是为庄襄王。庄襄王所母华阳后为华阳太后，真母夏姬尊以为夏太后。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: The King of Qin had been on the throne one year when he died; his posthumous title was Xiaowen. The Heir Apparent, Zichu, succeeded him; this was King Zhuangxiang. The one King Zhuangxiang had as his mother, Queen Huayang, became Queen Dowager Huayang, and his real mother, Lady Xia, was honoured as Queen Dowager Xia.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 赵将李牧大破匈奴十馀万骑，灭襜褴，破东胡，降林胡，单于奔走。 辨析：《史記·廉頗藺相如列傳》： 李牧者，赵之北边良将也。常居代雁门，备匈奴。以便宜置吏，市租皆输入莫府，为士卒费。日击数牛飨士，习射骑，谨烽火，多间谍，厚遇战士。为约曰：“匈奴即入盗，急入收保，有敢捕虏者斩。”匈奴每入，烽火谨，辄入收保，不敢战。如是数岁，亦不亡失。然匈奴以李牧为怯，虽赵边兵亦以为吾将怯。赵王让李牧，李牧如故。赵王怒，召之，使他人代将。 岁馀，匈奴每来，出战。出战，数不利，失亡多，边不得田畜。复请李牧。牧杜门不出，固称疾。赵王乃复强起使将兵。牧曰：“王必用臣，臣如前，乃敢奉令。”王许之。 李牧至，如故约。匈奴数岁无所得。终以为怯。边士日得赏赐而不用，皆原一战。於是乃具选车得千三百乘，选骑得万三千匹，百金之士五万人，彀者十万人，悉勒习战。大纵畜牧，人民满野。匈奴小入，详北不胜，以数千人委之。单于闻之，大率众来入。李牧多为奇陈，张左右翼击之，大破杀匈奴十馀万骑。灭襜褴，破东胡，降林胡，单于奔走。其後十馀岁，匈奴不敢近赵边城。 《史記·趙世家》載李牧為將是趙悼襄王二年（前243），李牧與匈奴的戰事年代不詳。又，《史記·匈奴列傳》：其后赵将李牧时，匈奴不敢入赵边。 李牧與匈奴的戰事或在趙悼襄王二年（前243）後。“其後十馀岁”或指趙悼襄王至秦滅趙的十餘年間。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Zhao general Li Mu heavily defeated more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen, destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled. Analysis: Shiji, Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru: Li Mu was a fine general of Zhao's northern frontier. He was regularly stationed at Yanmen in Dai, on guard against the Xiongnu. He appointed officers at his own discretion, and the market taxes were all paid into his headquarters for the soldiers' expenses. Every day he slaughtered several oxen to feast his men; he drilled them in archery and riding, kept careful watch on the beacon fires, used many spies, and treated the fighting men generously. He laid down a rule: "When the Xiongnu come in to raid, withdraw at once into the strongholds; anyone who dares to take captives will be beheaded." Whenever the Xiongnu came in, the beacons gave careful warning and the men withdrew at once into the strongholds and did not dare to fight. So it went for several years, and nothing was lost either. But the Xiongnu took Li Mu for a coward, and even the Zhao frontier troops thought their general a coward. The King of Zhao reproved Li Mu, but Li Mu went on as before. The King of Zhao was angry, recalled him, and had another man take over the command. After a year or more, whenever the Xiongnu came, the army went out to fight. Going out to fight, it was repeatedly worsted, the losses were many, and on the frontier there was no farming or herding. The king again asked for Li Mu. Mu shut his gate and would not come out, insisting that he was ill. The King of Zhao then pressed him again to rise and sent him to command the troops. Mu said: "If Your Majesty must employ your servant, your servant will dare to accept the command only if he may do as before." The king consented. Li Mu arrived and kept to the old rule. For several years the Xiongnu got nothing, and to the end they took him for a coward. The frontier soldiers received rewards every day and were never used, and all of them wished for a single battle. Thereupon he fitted out picked chariots, and got thirteen hundred; picked horsemen, and got thirteen thousand; soldiers of the hundred jin of gold, fifty thousand; and bowmen, a hundred thousand; and he drilled them all for battle. He let the herds out to graze far and wide, and the people filled the open country. The Xiongnu came in with a small force; he feigned defeat and abandoned several thousand men to them. When the Chanyu heard of it, he came in at the head of a great host. Li Mu set many unexpected formations, spread out his left and right wings and struck, and heavily defeated and killed more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen. He destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled. For more than ten years after that the Xiongnu did not dare to come near the frontier Fortresses of Zhao. The Shiji, Hereditary House of Zhao, records Li Mu as general in the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC); the date of Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu is not known. Further, the Shiji, Account of the Xiongnu: "Later, in the time of the Zhao general Li Mu, the Xiongnu did not dare to enter the Zhao frontier." Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu was perhaps after the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC). "For more than ten years after that" perhaps means the ten-odd years from King Daoxiang to Qin's destruction of Zhao.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 周本纪：后七岁，秦庄襄王灭东周。东西周皆入于秦，周既不祀。 秦本纪：庄襄王元年，大赦罪人，修先王功臣，施德厚骨肉而布惠于民。东周君与诸侯谋秦，秦使相国吕不韦诛之，尽入其国。秦不绝其祀，以阳人地赐周君，奉其祭祀。使蒙骜伐韩，韩献成皋、巩。秦界至大梁，初置三川郡。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Zhou: Seven years later, King Zhuangxiang of Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou. Eastern and Western Zhou both passed into Qin's hands, and Zhou's sacrifices ended altogether. Basic Annals of Qin: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he granted a great pardon to offenders, honoured the meritorious servants of the former kings, showed favour and generosity to his kin, and spread his bounty among the people. The Lord of Eastern Zhou plotted against Qin with the Lords; Qin sent the Chancellor of State Lü Buwei to punish him and took in the whole of his state. Qin did not cut off his sacrifices: it granted the Lord of Zhou the land of Yangren so that he might keep up his sacrifices. It sent Meng Ao to attack Han, and Han presented Chenggao and Gong. Qin's border reached to Daliang, and for the first time Sanchuan Commandery was established.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：蒙驚取成皋、榮陽，初置三川郡。呂不韋相，取東周。 韓：秦拔我成皋、榮陽。 楚：楚滅魯，頃公遷卞，為家人，絕祀。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Meng Ao took Chenggao and Xingyang; Sanchuan Commandery was established for the first time. Lü Buwei became Chancellor. Took Eastern Zhou. Han: Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang. Chu: Chu destroyed Lu; Duke Qing was moved to Bian, became a commoner, and the sacrifices were cut off.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 鲁周公世家：二十四年，楚考烈王伐灭鲁。顷公亡，迁于下邑，为家人，鲁绝祀。顷公卒于柯。 鲁起周公至顷公，凡三十四世。 燕召公世家：六年，秦灭东周，置三川郡。 赵世家：十七年，假相大将武襄君攻燕，围其国。 韩世家：二十四年，秦拔我城皋、荥阳。 田敬仲完世家：十六年，秦灭周。君王后卒。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of the Duke of Zhou of Lu: In the twenty-fourth year, King Kaolie of Chu attacked and destroyed Lu. Duke Qing fled and was moved to an outlying settlement; he became a commoner, and Lu's sacrifices were cut off. Duke Qing died at Ke. From the Duke of Zhou to Duke Qing, Lu had thirty-four generations in all. Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the sixth year, Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou and established Sanchuan Commandery. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the seventeenth year, the Acting Chancellor and great general Lord Wuxiang attacked Yan and besieged its capital. Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-fourth year, Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang. Hereditary House of Tian Jingzhong Wan: In the sixteenth year, Qin destroyed Zhou. Queen Jun died.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 春申君列传：春申君相十四年，秦庄襄王立，以吕不韦为相，封为文信侯。取东周。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Chunshen: In the fourteenth year of Lord Chunshen's chancellorship, King Zhuangxiang of Qin came to the throne; he made Lü Buwei Chancellor and enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin. Took Eastern Zhou.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传：庄襄王元年，以吕不韦为丞相，封为文信侯，食河南雒阳十万户。 蒙恬列传：蒙恬者，其先齐人也。恬大父蒙骜，自齐事秦昭王，官至上卿。秦庄襄王元年，蒙骜为秦将，伐韩，取成皋、荥阳，作置三川郡。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he made Lü Buwei Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin, and gave him Luoyang in Henan, a hundred thousand households, as his fief. Biography of Meng Tian: Meng Tian's forebears were men of Qi. Tian's grandfather Meng Ao came from Qi to serve King Zhao of Qin, and rose in office to Senior Minister. In the first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, Meng Ao was a general of Qin; he attacked Han, took Chenggao and Xingyang, and set up Sanchuan Commandery.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 春平侯担任赵相邦。 辨析：我國曾出土多件春平侯鈹，其中十件銘文刻“十七年，相邦春平侯”。據學者推斷，“十七年”是已知最早的年份，但春平侯何時開始擔任相邦，史書未載，且，趙國相邦應不止一人。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I Marquis Chunping served as Chancellor of State of Zhao. Analysis: A number of pi blades of Marquis Chunping have been excavated in China, ten of them inscribed "seventeenth year, Chancellor of State Marquis Chunping". Scholars infer that the "seventeenth year" is the earliest year known, but when Marquis Chunping began to serve as Chancellor of State the histories do not record; and moreover Zhao's Chancellors of State were presumably more than one.

passages.title: Other ancient works (histories)
passages.zh: 其他古籍（史類） 辨析：楚並瑯琊，遷越王親於吳。 越王勾践灭吴称霸是公元前473年，称霸224年越国灭亡，那就是-473+224=公元前249年 《越绝书·越绝外传记地传》: 越王夫镡以上至无余，久远，世不可纪也。夫镡子允常。允常子勾践，大霸称王，徙琅琊，都也。勾践子与夷，时霸。与夷子子翁，时霸。子翁子不扬，时霸。不扬子无彊，时霸，伐楚，威王灭无彊。无彊子之侯，窃自立为君长。之侯子尊，时君长。尊子亲，失众，楚伐之，走南山。亲以上至勾践，凡八君，都琅琊二百二十四岁。无彊以上霸，称王。之侯以下微弱，称君长。 《吴越春秋》（勾践伐吴外传第十） 二十七年冬，勾践寝疾将卒，谓太子兴夷曰：“吾自禹之后，承元常之德，蒙天灵之祐，神祗之福，从穷越之地籍，楚之前锋，以摧吴王之干戈。跨江涉淮，从晋齐之地，功德巍巍。自致于斯，其可不诫乎？夫霸者之后，难以久立，其慎之哉！”遂卒。 兴夷即位一年卒，子翁；翁卒，子不扬；不扬卒，子无强；强卒，子玉；玉卒，子尊；尊卒，子亲。自勾践至于亲，其历八主，皆称霸，积年二百二十四年，亲众皆失，而去琅邪，徙于吴矣。 自黄帝至少康十世，自禹受禅至少康即位六世，为一百四十四年，少康去颛顼即位，四百二十四年。 黄帝→昌意→颛顼→鲧→禹→启→太康→仲庐→相→少康→无余→无壬（去无余十世）→无曎→夫谭→元常→勾践→兴夷→不寿→不扬→无强→鲁穆柳有幽公为名，王侯自称为君→尊→亲，失琅邪，为楚所灭。 勾践至王亲，历八主，格霸二百二十四年。从无余越国始封，至余善返越国空灭，凡一千九百二十二年。 《续汉书·郡国志四》，刘昭在“吴郡安县”一条下注道: 《越绝》曰，有西岑冢，越王孙开所立，以备春申君，使其子守之，子死遂葬城中。 春申君公元前248年被封于江东(《史记·春申君列传》。由此可知，在公元前三世纪半，江浙地区还存在不服从楚国的越势力。 两位专家告诉记者，连云港锦屏山九龙口古城址，考古界称其为尾矿坝遗址，此前未曾有人将其与越王迁都之地联系在一起。他们通过实地调查发现，遗址是一处周长约十里的古代城址。其城三面环山，东面朝大海。城中已被锦屏山左的磷矿废矿砂所填平，形成方圆十余里、深约20余米的积沙。今露出城中部的当时一高台地尚存，南北长300米，东西宽150米左右。考古学家在此台地表采集到了大量越国风格的陶片残器，经检测均为春秋晚期、战国早期的印纹硬陶。由此证实这些遗物当属越国。 随后，专家又在杜佑的《唐·通典》中找到了锦屏山又叫琅琊山的依据。根据史料记载，锦屏山在秦朝建立之前称朐山，又叫琅琊山。秦始皇时期，立为朐县，秦始皇35年（公元前212年）立石为秦东门。秦始皇28年，秦始皇又在山东筑起琅琊台与琅琊邑相呼应。张志立、彭云认为，由于地名的变迁，琅琊山之名渐渐淡出，许多人由此把越王勾践迁都连云港琅琊山的地点误当作了山东青岛地区胶南市的琅琊山。
passages.en: Other ancient works (histories) Analysis: Chu annexed Langya and moved King Qin of Yue to Wu. King Goujian of Yue destroyed Wu and became hegemon in 473 BC; the state of Yue perished after 224 years of hegemony, which gives −473 + 224 = 249 BC Yuejueshu, Outer Tradition, Record of the Lands: From King Futan of Yue back to Wuyu is remote and far off, and the generations cannot be recorded. Futan's son was Yunchang. Yunchang's son was Goujian, who was a great hegemon and styled himself king; he moved to Langya and made it his capital. Goujian's son Yuyi was hegemon in his time. Yuyi's son Ziweng was hegemon in his time. Ziweng's son Buyang was hegemon in his time. Buyang's son Wujiang was hegemon in his time; he attacked Chu, and King Wei destroyed Wujiang. Wujiang's son Zhihou set himself up without warrant as chieftain. Zhihou's son Zun was chieftain in his time. Zun's son Qin lost his people; Chu attacked him and he fled to the southern hills. From Qin back to Goujian, eight lords in all, had their capital at Langya for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wujiang upward they were hegemons and styled themselves king; from Zhihou downward they were weak and were styled chieftains. Wu Yue Chunqiu (Outer Tradition of Goujian's Attack on Wu, chapter ten) In the winter of the twenty-seventh year, Goujian lay ill and was about to die, and said to the Heir Apparent Xingyi: "I, descended from Yu, inheriting the virtue of Yuanchang, blessed by the protection of Heaven's spirits and the favour of the gods, from the land of poor and remote Yue, with Chu as my vanguard, broke the shields and spears of the King of Wu. I crossed the Jiang and forded the Huai, passed through the lands of Jin and Qi, and my merit and virtue stood towering. Having brought myself to this, can one fail to take warning? The heirs of a hegemon find it hard to stand for long; be careful of it!" Then he died. Xingyi came to the throne and died after one year; his son was Weng. Weng died; his son was Buyang. Buyang died; his son was Wuqiang. Qiang died; his son was Yu. Yu died; his son was Zun. Zun died; his son was Qin. From Goujian down to Qin there were eight rulers, all styled hegemon, over two hundred and twenty-four years in all; Qin lost all his people, left Langya and moved to Wu. From the Yellow Emperor to Shaokang were ten generations; from Yu's receiving the abdication to Shaokang's accession were six generations, one hundred and forty-four years; from Shaokang back to Zhuanxu's accession, four hundred and twenty-four years. Yellow Emperor → Changyi → Zhuanxu → Gun → Yu → Qi → Taikang → Zhonglu → Xiang → Shaokang → Wuyu → Wuren (ten generations from Wuyu) → Wuyi → Futan → Yuanchang → Goujian → Xingyi → Bushou → Buyang → Wuqiang → Lu Mu Liu, who had Duke You as his name; kings and marquises styled themselves lords → Zun → Qin, who lost Langya and was destroyed by Chu. From Goujian to King Qin, eight rulers, hegemons for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wuyu's first enfeoffment in Yue to Yushan's return and the emptying and extinction of the state of Yue, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two years in all. In the Xu Hanshu, Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms IV, Liu Zhao notes under the entry "An County, Wu Commandery": The Yuejue says: there is the Xicen tomb, set up by Kai, grandson of the King of Yue, to guard against Lord Chunshen; he had his son hold it, and when the son died he was buried within the Fortress. Lord Chunshen was enfeoffed in Jiangdong in 248 BC (Shiji, Biography of Lord Chunshen). From this it can be known that in the middle of the third century BC there were still Yue forces in the Jiangsu–Zhejiang region that did not submit to Chu. The two experts told the reporter that the ancient walled site at Jiulongkou on Jinpingshan, Lianyungang, which archaeologists call the tailings-dam site, had never before been connected with the place to which the King of Yue moved his capital. By survey on the ground they found the site to be an ancient walled city about ten li in circumference. The city is ringed by hills on three sides and faces the sea on the east. Its interior has been filled by the waste sand of the phosphate mine to the left of Jinpingshan, forming an accumulation of sand more than ten li round and some twenty metres deep. A raised terrace of the period, now exposed in the middle of the city, survives, about 300 metres from north to south and some 150 metres from east to west. On this terrace archaeologists collected a great many pottery sherds and fragments of vessels in the Yue style, all identified on examination as stamped hard pottery of the late Spring and Autumn and early Warring States periods, which confirmed that these remains belong to Yue. The experts then found in Du You's Tongdian of the Tang the basis for Jinpingshan's other name, Langyashan. According to the historical records, before the Qin dynasty was founded Jinpingshan was called Qushan, also Langyashan. In the time of the First Emperor of Qin it was made Qu County, and in his thirty-fifth year (212 BC) a stone was set up there as Qin's eastern gate. In his twenty-eighth year the First Emperor also built the Langya Terrace in Shandong, to answer to the Langya settlement. Zhang Zhili and Peng Yun hold that, with the changes of place-names, the name Langyashan gradually fell out of use, and many people have therefore mistaken the place to which King Goujian of Yue moved his capital, Langyashan at Lianyungang, for the Langyashan of Jiaonan city in the Qingdao region of Shandong.

passages.en: Qin slips in the Yuelu Academy collection In the time of the Grand Supreme Emperor the Clerk of the Capital said: The sikou, the yinguan and those serving their geng turn at the Western Workshop are many of them poor and cannot provide their own grain. Deliberation: Let the Counties send the sikou to deliver grain; where a County has no grain to be lent, let it report to the County of the work-site for repayment and loan. The Western Workshop fells timber in the hills of Ju and Nanzheng; let Ju and Nanzheng act on the Western Workshop's requisitions. Those who deliver the grain, and the officers, are passed on to the Western Workshop. · In the second year it was said: Put back in use.

passages.zh: 附：《戰國縱橫家書》原文 附：《贱臣筡西问秦王》： 贱臣筡西问秦王，曰：“王之外訄臣筡（愿）欲得王之倚立之閒（闲），渴（竭）腹之所闻。当今□之时，衍……巍（魏）五邦相与，陟＝若壹，为义虖（乎）？筡弗得智（知）；不为（正1）义虖（乎）？筡有（又）弗能智（知），不识吾王将可（何）以侍（待）之？”王不合（答）。筡有（又）称曰：“五邦以义来甗（献），吾王以义侍（待）之，不为义虖（乎）？（愿）吾王有以义侍（待）之者。为义者，皆欲人之以（正2）义也。”王有（又）不合（答）。筡有（又）曰：“欲有复言也，恐刀居（锯）不容于身。”王曰：“先生言也，寡人谨听。”筡曰：“今夫桀肘（纣）贵为天子，富有天下，尽已失之矣。无异故，皆以（正3）不义反为义者也。巍（魏）人与越人战宿胥之壄（野），而栖越王廥（会）稽廥纂之上；当此时，吴人侵（寝）兵立义事鬼，强为天子，吴人不侵（寝）兵立义事鬼，（正4）尽已失其先王冢庙及与大都连者。无异故，皆以不义反为义者也。今筡入，王之四竞（境）者（诸）民皆有（蚀）寒之色，窃问其故，曰：‘壹恶用兵矣。’阴晋、上雒（洛）之（正5）卒，天下之良卒也，自酆綦以来，夫斩首六矣。今出战不能胜，而内守不能箇（固），不能守其城郭而五刑传其身，而弗能佴（耻）也。无异故，皆未罢也。干将、莫冶（邪），（正6）天下之良剑也，金试□兔（？）壶（？）□□□□□……□勿绎（释）……[马录]耳，天下之良马也，重载以驰于路久而勿绎（释），骀马（正7）□至。无异故，皆未罢也。攻军杀将，王之（禄）也，者（诸）民之力也。者（诸）民绳身以断剅（头）列（裂）腹，宛取□□身以（迁）徙忧守之，此亦大过（祸）矣。万乘王所以□[于]□（背1），或欲黄金朱（珠）玉走马□猎听乐，是以闻谈说之士言攻（击）之便，得地之利，约车众者数百[乘]，而□者数十乘，齎（赍）币帛以□者（诸）侯，必旦兴师□（背2）以□边竞（境）。丈夫居军不□□□□□□□责阵卒，久者数岁，□者期年。兴而治地，地方环（圆）不□百余里，而地有不可虚，必且（迁）中□（背3）之民以实之，百姓弗安且茗，可虖（乎）？王胡不止兵毋兴令居，允其图（？）□，修其垣蘠（墙），又且相□，居得其乐而陈责皆赏。以筡之私此，此天下之良（背4）策已。黄啻□曰行年三百□椯（端）身□察乃智（知）足。今吾王之地，东南囊（？）楚而北半赵，是皆[膏]臾（腴）之地也。西尽日入之所，到无甲之□，而兵强人众莫弗（背5）智（知）已。有＝（又有）最奡、必方、婴（樱）母（梅）、橘鼬（柚）、毗（枇）杷、茈橿（姜）之林，鐘蠪胥（蹇）之州，美丹之穴，赣勒、□□、敝稯（椶）、桃支（枝）之渚，而万物无不有已。”（背6）
passages.en: Appendix: text of the Zhanguo zonghengjia shu Appendix: Your humble servant Tu went west to put questions to the King of Qin: Your humble servant Tu went west and put questions to the King of Qin, saying: "Your servant Tu, pressing from without, wishes to have a moment of Your Majesty's standing leisure, to pour out all that his belly holds of what he has heard. At the present □ time, Yan…… Wei and the five states are joined together and advance as one. Is this for righteousness? Tu cannot know. Is it not for righteousness? Tu again cannot know, and does not know with what my King will meet it." The King did not answer. Tu again declared: "If the five states come with righteousness to make their offer, and my King meets them with righteousness, is that not righteousness? I wish my King had the means to meet them with righteousness. Those who act for righteousness all wish others to act towards them with righteousness." The King again did not answer. Tu again said: "I wish to speak further, but fear the knife and saw will not spare my body." The King said: "Speak, sir; I listen with care." Tu said: "Now Jie and Zhou were honoured as Sons of Heaven and rich in all under heaven, and lost it all. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. The men of Wei fought the men of Yue in the wilds of Suxu, and perched the King of Yue on the summit of Kuaiji; at that time the men of Wu laid down their arms, established righteousness and served the spirits, and forced their way to be Son of Heaven; when the men of Wu did not lay down their arms, establish righteousness and serve the spirits, they lost it all, the tombs and temples of their former kings and whatever joined the great capital. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. Now as Tu came in, the people within Your Majesty's four borders all had the look of hunger and cold; I privately asked the reason, and they said: 'How we hate the use of arms!' The soldiers of Yinjin and Shangluo are the finest soldiers under heaven; since Fengqi they have taken heads six times. Now going out to battle they cannot win, and keeping guard within they cannot hold firm; they cannot hold their walls, and the five punishments pass over their bodies, yet they cannot feel it as shame. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. Ganjiang and Moye are the finest swords under heaven; tried on metal □ … □□□□□□ … never let go …; Lü'er is the finest horse under heaven; driven on the road under heavy loads for long and never let go, a worn-out nag □ arrives. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. To attack armies and kill generals is the King's gain, but it is the people's strength. The people put their bodies to the cord to have their heads cut off and their bellies ripped; … taken □□ bodies, moved away to garrison in anxious guard, this too is a great calamity. That by which a king of ten thousand chariots □ [on] □ □: some desire gold, pearls and jade, racing horses, □ hunting and listening to music, and so, hearing the persuaders tell of the ease of attack and the profit of gaining land, the great among them pledge several hundred [chariots] and the □ several tens, and carry silks and gifts to □ the Lords; and surely next morning they raise an army □ to □ the border. The men who stay in the army do not □□□□□□□ … the ranks: the longest for several years, the □ for a full year. The levy raised and the land brought under rule, a territory not □ a hundred-odd li around, and land that cannot be left empty, so that the people of the interior □ must be moved to fill it; the common people are not at ease and moreover □: can this be? Why does the King not halt the troops and raise none, and order them to stay at home, grant them their plans (?) □, repair their walls, and further □ one another, so that at home they have their joy and the arrears of levies are all rewarded? In Tu's private view, this is the finest policy under heaven. The Yellow Emperor □ said: at three hundred years of age □, straighten the body, □ examine, and then know sufficiency. Now my King's land bags (?) Chu to the south-east and halves Zhao to the north, all of it [fertile] land. To the west it reaches where the sun goes in, to the □ of no armour; that its soldiers are strong and its people many, none does not know. It has besides forests of zui'ao, bifang, cherry and plum, orange and pomelo, loquat and purple ginger; islets of zhonglong and xujian; caves of fine cinnabar; and shoals of ganle, □□, palm and peach-branch; of the myriad things there is none it lacks."

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：二年，使蒙骜攻赵，定太原。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the second year he sent Meng Ao to attack Zhao and settled Taiyuan.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：蒙驚擊趙榆次、新城、狼孟， 得三十七城。 日蝕。 楚：春申君徙封於吳。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Meng Ao struck Zhao's Yuci, Xincheng and Langmeng, and took thirty-seven Fortresses. Eclipse of the sun. Chu: Lord Chunshen's fief was moved to Wu.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 燕召公世家：七年，秦拔赵榆次三十七城，秦置大原郡。 赵世家：十八年，延陵钧率师从相国信平君助魏攻燕。秦拔我榆次三十七城。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the seventh year, Qin took Zhao's Yuci and thirty-seven Fortresses; Qin set up Taiyuan Commandery. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the eighteenth year, Yanling Jun led an army under the Chancellor of State Lord Xinping to help Wei attack Yan. Qin took our Yuci and thirty-seven Fortresses.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 春申君列传：考烈王元年，以黄歇为相，封为春申君，赐淮北地十二县。後十五岁，黄歇言之楚王曰：“淮北地边齐，其事急，请以为郡便。”因并献淮北十二县。请封於江东。考烈王许之。春申君因城故吴墟，以自为都邑。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Chunshen: In the first year of King Kaolie he made Huang Xie Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Lord Chunshen, and granted him twelve Counties of the land north of the Huai. Fifteen years later Huang Xie said to the King of Chu: "The land north of the Huai borders Qi, and its affairs are pressing; it would be better made a Commandery." And he gave back the twelve Counties north of the Huai, asking to be enfeoffed in Jiangdong. King Kaolie consented. Lord Chunshen accordingly fortified the old ruins of Wu and made them his seat.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 蒙恬列传：二年，蒙骜攻赵，取三十七城。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Meng Tian: In the second year Meng Ao attacked Zhao and took thirty-seven Fortresses.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 秦将井忌助赵攻燕，拔二城。 辨析：事見《戰國縱橫家書》，但是時間不詳： 二十五、李园谓辛梧章 秦使辛梧据粱（梁），合秦粱（梁）而攻楚。李园忧之。兵未出，谓辛梧：“以秦之强，有两端之劲，东面而伐楚。于臣也，楚不侍（待）伐割挚马免而西走，秦余（与）楚为上交，秦祸案环（还）中粱（梁）矣。将军必逐于粱（梁），恐诛于秦。 将军不见井忌乎？为秦据赵而攻燕，拔二城。燕使蔡鸟股符〓去壁，奸（间）赵入秦，以河间十城封秦相文信侯。文信侯弗敢受，曰：‘我无功。’ 蔡鸟明日见，带长剑，举其末，视视（示）文信侯曰：‘君曰我无功，君无功，胡不解君之玺，以佩蒙敖（骜）、王〓也？秦王以君为贤，故加君二人之上。今燕献地。此非秦之地也。君弗受，不忠。’文信侯敬若（诺）。言之秦王，秦王令受之。余（与）燕为上交，秦祸案环（还）归于赵矣。秦大举兵东面而赍赵，言毋攻燕。以秦之强，有燕之怒，割勺（赵）必深。赵不能听，逐井忌，诛于秦。今臣窃为将军私计，不如少案（按）之，毋庸出兵，秦未得志于楚，必重粱（梁），粱（梁）未得志于楚，必重秦，是将军两重。天下人无不死者，久者寿。愿将军之察之也。粱（梁）兵未出，楚见粱（梁）之未出兵也，走秦必缓。秦王怒于楚之缓也，怨必深。是将军有（又）重矣。”粱（梁）兵果六月乃出。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Qin general Jing Ji helped Zhao attack Yan and took two Fortresses. Analysis: the matter is seen in the Zhanguo zonghengjia shu, but the time is not known: Chapter 25, Li Yuan speaks to Xin Wu Qin sent Xin Wu to hold Liang, to join Qin and Liang in an attack on Chu. Li Yuan was troubled by this. Before the troops had set out he said to Xin Wu: "With Qin's strength and the force of two arms, you face east and attack Chu. As your servant sees it, Chu will not wait to be attacked: it will cede land and bring gifts and hurry west, Qin and Chu will become the closest of allies, and Qin's blow will then fall back upon Liang. The General will surely be driven out of Liang, and I fear put to death by Qin. Has the General not seen the case of Jing Ji? On Qin's behalf he held Zhao and attacked Yan, taking two Fortresses. Yan sent Cai Niao, who with a tally made his way out through the ramparts, passed secretly through Zhao into Qin and offered the ten Fortresses of Hejian as a fief to the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Wenxin. Marquis Wenxin did not dare accept, saying: 'I have no merit.' The next day Cai Niao came to see him wearing a long sword, raised its point and showed it to Marquis Wenxin, saying: 'You say "I have no merit". If you have no merit, why not untie your seal and hang it on Meng Ao or Wang 〓? The King of Qin holds you worthy, and so has set you above those two. Now Yan offers land; this is not Qin's land. If you do not accept it, you are disloyal.' Marquis Wenxin respectfully agreed. He spoke of it to the King of Qin, and the King of Qin ordered him to accept. Qin became Yan's closest ally, and Qin's blow then turned back upon Zhao. Qin raised a great army, faced east and bore down on Zhao, declaring that Yan was not to be attacked. With Qin's strength and Yan's anger, the cutting of Zhao was bound to go deep. Zhao could not bear it; it drove out Jing Ji, and he was put to death by Qin. Now, if your servant may privately plan for the General: better to hold back a little and not send out the troops. So long as Qin has not had its way with Chu, it must value Liang; so long as Liang has not had its way with Chu, it must value Qin — thus the General is valued on both sides. No man under Heaven escapes death; he who lasts long lives long. I wish the General to consider it. While Liang's troops have not set out, Chu, seeing that Liang has not sent out its troops, will be slow to hurry to Qin. The King of Qin, angered at Chu's slowness, will resent it deeply; and so the General is valued still more." Liang's troops did indeed set out only after six months.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）二 燕献河间十城于秦相吕不韦，秦庄襄王令吕不韦受地，兴兵胁迫赵国“毋攻燕”，赵孝成王不听。 辨析：事見《戰國縱橫家書》，但是時間不詳： 二十五、李园谓辛梧章（左側） 赵相邦春平侯、平国君先后入秦，被秦庄襄王留为人质。 辨析：此應根據《戰國策·秦召春平侯》，但原文並未說明具體時間。 又：《論春平侯及其相關問題》：平都侯当即铍铭所见的“平国君”。文献以“都”换“国”字的情况，跟文献所见的“信平君”、“建信君”之“信”，铍铭都写作“躬(躬)”类似。 又：《史記·趙世家》把此事歸在趙悼襄王二年。 赵孝成王命信平君廉颇担任相邦。 辨析：此應根據《史記·趙世家》，廉颇在趙孝成王十五年已擔任守相。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II Yan offered the ten Fortresses of Hejian to the Chancellor of Qin, Lü Buwei; King Zhuangxiang of Qin ordered Lü Buwei to accept the land, and raised troops to press Zhao "not to attack Yan"; King Xiaocheng of Zhao did not comply. Analysis: the matter is seen in the Zhanguo zonghengjia shu, but the time is not known: Chapter 25, Li Yuan speaks to Xin Wu (at left) Zhao's Chancellor of State Marquis Chunping and Lord Pingguo went into Qin one after the other and were kept by King Zhuangxiang of Qin as hostages. Analysis: this should rest on the Zhanguoce, "Qin summons Marquis Chunping", but the original text does not give the time. Further, from "On Marquis Chunping and the questions connected with him": Marquis Pingdu must be the "Lord Pingguo" seen in the pi-blade inscriptions. The texts' putting 都 for 国 is like the 信 of the texts' "Lord Xinping" and "Lord Jianxin", which the pi inscriptions all write 躬 (躬). Further: the Hereditary House of Zhao in the Shiji places this matter in the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao. King Xiaocheng of Zhao appointed Lord Xinping, Lian Po, Chancellor of State. Analysis: this should rest on the Hereditary House of Zhao in the Shiji, where Lian Po was already Acting Chancellor in the fifteenth year of King Xiaocheng.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：三年，蒙骜攻魏高都、汲，拔之。攻赵榆次、新城、狼孟，取三十七城。四月日食。王龁攻上党。初置太原郡。魏将无忌率五国兵击秦，秦却于河外。蒙骜败，解而去。五月丙午，庄襄王卒，子政立，是为秦始皇帝。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the third year Meng Ao attacked Wei's Gaodu and Ji and took them. He attacked Zhao's Yuci, Xincheng and Langmeng and took thirty-seven Fortresses. In April there was an eclipse of the sun. Wang He attacked Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time. The Wei general Wuji led the troops of five states against Qin, and Qin fell back to Hewai. Meng Ao was defeated, broke off and withdrew. In May, on the day Bingwu, King Zhuangxiang died, and his son Zheng was set up: this was the First Emperor of Qin.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：王齮擊上黨。初置太原郡。 魏公子無忌率五國卻我軍河外，蒙驁解去。 魏：無忌率五國兵敗秦軍河外。 韓：秦拔我上黨。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Wang Yi struck Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time. Prince Wuji of Wei led five states and drove our army back at Hewai; Meng Ao broke off and withdrew. Wei: Wuji led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai. Han: Qin took our Shangdang.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 楚世家：十六年，秦庄襄王卒，秦王赵政立。 赵世家：十九年，赵与燕易土：以龙兑、汾门、临乐与燕；燕以葛、武阳、平舒与赵。 魏世家：三十年，无忌归魏，率五国兵攻秦，败之河外，走蒙骜。魏太子增质於秦，秦怒，欲囚魏太子增。或为增谓秦王曰：“公孙喜固谓魏相曰‘请以魏疾击秦，秦王怒，必囚增。魏王又怒，击秦，秦必伤’。今王囚增，是喜之计中也。故不若贵增而合魏，以疑之於齐、韩。”秦乃止增。 韩世家：二十六年，秦悉拔我上党。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Chu: In the sixteenth year, King Zhuangxiang of Qin died, and the King of Qin, Zhao Zheng, was set up. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the nineteenth year, Zhao and Yan exchanged land: Zhao gave Longdui, Fenmen and Linle to Yan, and Yan gave Ge, Wuyang and Pingshu to Zhao. Hereditary House of Wei: In the thirtieth year, Wuji returned to Wei, led the troops of five states to attack Qin, defeated them at Hewai and put Meng Ao to flight. The Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng, was a hostage in Qin; Qin was angered and wished to imprison the Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng. Someone said to the King of Qin on Zeng's behalf: "Gongsun Xi firmly told the Chancellor of Wei: 'Let Wei attack Qin hard; the King of Qin will be angered and will surely imprison Zeng. The King of Wei will be angered in turn and attack Qin, and Qin will surely be hurt.' Now if the King imprisons Zeng, Xi's plan has hit its mark. So it is better to honour Zeng and ally with Wei, so as to make Qi and Han suspicious of it." Qin thereupon let Zeng be. Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-sixth year, Qin took all our Shangdang.
